wordings.title: Most common words
wordings.statement:
Write `top_words(text, k)`. A word is a run of the letters `a` to `z`, ignoring case,
that may have apostrophes inside it, like `don't`. Every other character separates
words. Return the `k` most common words, in lowercase, as `(word, count)` pairs, most
common first. Words with equal counts come in the order they first appear in the text.
When there are fewer than `k` different words, return them all.

examples.input: top_words("The cat and the hat. THE END, don't stop", 2)
examples.explanation: cat, and, hat, end, don't and stop each appear once; cat comes first.

problems.tests:
import random

from solution import *


def test_example_1():
    """Case is ignored; equal counts keep the order of first appearance."""
    assert top_words("The cat and the hat. THE END, don't stop", 2) == [('the', 3), ('cat', 1)]


def test_apostrophes():
    """Apostrophes count only inside a word."""
    assert top_words("'tis the dogs' don't don't", 3) == [("don't", 2), ('tis', 1), ('the', 1)]


def test_separators():
    """Digits, hyphens and underscores separate words."""
    assert top_words('a1b-c_d a', 10) == [('a', 2), ('b', 1), ('c', 1), ('d', 1)]


def test_empty():
    """No words, and k of 0."""
    assert top_words('', 3) == []
    assert top_words('... 123 !!!', 3) == []
    assert top_words('some words', 0) == []


def test_fewer_than_k():
    """All words when there are fewer than k."""
    assert top_words('b a b', 10) == [('b', 2), ('a', 1)]


def test_large():
    """A long text with known counts."""
    rng = random.Random(1)
    words = [chr(97 + i % 26) + chr(97 + i // 26) for i in range(500)]
    counts = {word: rng.randint(1, 200) for word in words}
    tokens = [word for word, count in counts.items() for _ in range(count)]
    rng.shuffle(tokens)
    first = {word: index for index, word in reversed(list(enumerate(tokens)))}
    text = ' '.join(token.upper() for token in tokens)
    expected = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], first[pair[0]]))
    assert top_words(text, 50) == expected[:50]
hints: Lowercase the text first, then a regular expression finds the words: re.findall returns every match. Letters with apostrophes between them: [a-z]+(?:'[a-z]+)*.
collections.Counter counts the items of any iterable.
Counter.most_common(k) returns the k most common (item, count) pairs, and equal counts keep the order in which items were first counted.
problems.summary: Count words with re and Counter

wordings.title: Merge sorted logs
wordings.statement:
Write `merge_logs(*logs)`. Each log is a list of lines `"<time> <message>"`, sorted by
time. The time is in ISO 8601 with an offset from UTC, such as
`2024-05-01T10:00:00+02:00`; UTC may also be written `Z`. Logs may use different
offsets.

Return all lines in one list, sorted by the moment they happened. Lines of the same
moment come in the order of their logs in the arguments, and in their order within a
log.

examples.explanation: In UTC the web lines are at 08:00 and 08:30, both before 09:00.

problems.tests:
import random
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from solution import *


def test_example_1():
    """Offsets decide the order, not the text of the times."""
    assert merge_logs(
        ['2024-05-01T10:00:00+02:00 web started', '2024-05-01T10:30:00+02:00 web ready'],
        ['2024-05-01T09:00:00Z db started'],
    ) == [
        '2024-05-01T10:00:00+02:00 web started',
        '2024-05-01T10:30:00+02:00 web ready',
        '2024-05-01T09:00:00Z db started',
    ]


def test_no_logs():
    """No logs, and empty logs."""
    assert merge_logs() == []
    assert merge_logs([], []) == []


def test_one_log():
    """A single log comes back as it is."""
    log = ['2024-01-01T00:00:00Z a', '2024-01-01T00:00:01Z b']
    assert merge_logs(log) == log


def test_same_moment():
    """Equal moments keep the order of the logs, then the order within each log."""
    first = ['2024-01-01T12:00:00+01:00 first-1', '2024-01-01T12:00:00+01:00 first-2']
    second = ['2024-01-01T11:00:00Z second']
    assert merge_logs(second, first) == ['2024-01-01T11:00:00Z second', *first]
    assert merge_logs(first, second) == [*first, '2024-01-01T11:00:00Z second']


def test_across_midnight():
    """A negative offset moves a line to the next day in UTC."""
    assert merge_logs(
        ['2024-03-01T23:30:00-05:00 late'], ['2024-03-02T01:00:00Z early']
    ) == ['2024-03-02T01:00:00Z early', '2024-03-01T23:30:00-05:00 late']


def test_messages_with_spaces():
    """Messages may contain spaces."""
    line = '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z disk is 90% full'
    assert merge_logs([line]) == [line]


def test_many():
    """Ten logs of 2,000 lines, each with its own offset."""
    rng = random.Random(9)
    start = datetime(2024, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    logs, moments = [], {}
    for number in range(10):
        zone = timezone(timedelta(hours=rng.randint(-12, 14)))
        seconds = sorted(rng.randint(0, 50000) for _ in range(2000))
        log = []
        for index, second in enumerate(seconds):
            moment = start + timedelta(seconds=second)
            line = f'{moment.astimezone(zone).isoformat()} log {number} line {index}'
            log.append(line)
            moments[line] = (moment, number, index)
        logs.append(log)
    assert merge_logs(*logs) == sorted(moments, key=moments.get)
hints: datetime.fromisoformat reads these times, offsets and Z included, and datetimes with offsets compare by the moment they stand for.
heapq.merge merges sorted iterables lazily and takes a key function, like sorted.
For equal keys, heapq.merge takes items from earlier iterables first, so the order of the logs is kept. The time is the text before the first space.
problems.summary: Merge sorted streams by aware datetimes

wordings.title: Count events in a time range
wordings.statement:
Write the class `Timeline`:

- `add(time)` records an event at `time`, an integer; events come in any order, and
  several may share a time
- `count(start, end)` returns how many events happened at a time from `start` to
  `end`, both included

`count` makes O(log n) comparisons for n events: it doesn't look at every event.

examples.input: t = Timeline(); t.add(5); t.add(1); t.add(5); t.count(2, 5)

problems.tests:
import random

from solution import *

_comparisons = 0


def _compare(operator):
    def compare(self, other):
        global _comparisons
        _comparisons += 1
        return getattr(int(self), operator)(int(other))

    return compare


class _Counted(int):
    """An integer that counts the comparisons it takes part in."""

    __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__, __eq__, __ne__ = (
        _compare(name) for name in ('__lt__', '__le__', '__gt__', '__ge__', '__eq__', '__ne__')
    )
    __hash__ = int.__hash__


def test_example_1():
    """Two events share a time inside the range."""
    t = Timeline()
    for time in (5, 1, 5):
        t.add(time)
    assert t.count(2, 5) == 2


def test_example_2():
    """A range after every event."""
    t = Timeline()
    for time in (5, 1, 5):
        t.add(time)
    assert t.count(6, 9) == 0


def test_empty():
    """No events at all."""
    assert Timeline().count(-10, 10) == 0


def test_ends_included():
    """Events exactly at start and end count."""
    t = Timeline()
    for time in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        t.add(time)
    assert t.count(2, 3) == 2
    assert t.count(4, 4) == 1
    assert t.count(1, 4) == 4


def test_separate_timelines():
    """Each timeline has its own events."""
    a, b = Timeline(), Timeline()
    a.add(1)
    assert (a.count(0, 2), b.count(0, 2)) == (1, 0)


def test_random():
    """Random events and ranges, compared with counting by hand."""
    rng = random.Random(4)
    t, times = Timeline(), []
    for _ in range(2000):
        time = rng.randint(-500, 500)
        t.add(time)
        times.append(time)
        start = rng.randint(-600, 600)
        end = start + rng.randint(0, 300)
        assert t.count(start, end) == sum(start <= x <= end for x in times)


def test_logarithmic_count():
    """With 20,000 events, a count makes a few dozen comparisons."""
    global _comparisons
    t = Timeline()
    for time in range(20000):
        t.add(_Counted(time * 7 % 20000))
    _comparisons = 0
    assert t.count(_Counted(250), _Counted(749)) == 500
    assert _comparisons <= 80
hints: Keep the times in a sorted list. bisect.insort inserts a value at its sorted position.
In a sorted list, bisect_left(a, x) is the index of the first item >= x, and bisect_right(a, x) the index after the last item <= x.
The count is bisect_right(times, end) - bisect_left(times, start): two binary searches.
problems.summary: Binary search a sorted list with bisect

wordings.title: CSV to JSON
wordings.statement:
Write `csv_to_json(text)`. `text` is CSV: a header row, then one row per record, with
fields quoted as the `csv` module reads them, so a quoted field may contain commas,
quotes and line breaks.

Return a JSON string: a list with an object per record, its keys the header names in
header order. A value made of the digits 0 to 9, with an optional minus sign before
them, like `-12`, becomes a number; an empty value becomes `null`; every other value
stays a string, unchanged.
constraints: Every record has as many fields as the header

hints: csv.DictReader reads rows as dicts keyed by the header, in header order. It needs lines to read: io.StringIO(text) turns the string into a file-like object.
Splitting the text on line breaks yourself would cut quoted fields that contain one.
Convert each value with a small function: None for '', int for a match of re.fullmatch(r'-?[0-9]+', value), else the string. json.dumps writes the list.
problems.summary: Read CSV with csv and io, write JSON with json

wordings.title: Run-length encoding
wordings.statement:
Write two functions:

- `encode(text)` returns the runs of equal characters in `text` as a list of
  `(character, length)` pairs
- `decode(runs)` turns such a list back into the text

`decode(encode(text))` gives back `text`.

problems.tests:
import random

from solution import *


def test_example_1():
    """Runs of several lengths."""
    assert encode('aaabccdddd') == [('a', 3), ('b', 1), ('c', 2), ('d', 4)]


def test_example_2():
    """Pairs back to text."""
    assert decode([('x', 2), ('y', 1)]) == 'xxy'


def test_empty():
    """Empty text, empty list."""
    assert encode('') == []
    assert decode([]) == ''


def test_runs_apart():
    """The same character in separate runs."""
    assert encode('aabaa') == [('a', 2), ('b', 1), ('a', 2)]


def test_no_runs():
    """Every character differs from the next."""
    assert encode('abc') == [('a', 1), ('b', 1), ('c', 1)]


def test_long_run():
    """A million equal characters."""
    assert encode('z' * 1000000) == [('z', 1000000)]
    assert decode([('z', 1000000)]) == 'z' * 1000000


def test_round_trip():
    """Random text survives encoding and decoding."""
    rng = random.Random(2)
    for _ in range(200):
        text = ''.join(rng.choice('ab ✓') * rng.randint(1, 4) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 50)))
        runs = encode(text)
        assert decode(runs) == text
        assert all(a[0] != b[0] for a, b in zip(runs, runs[1:]))
hints: itertools.groupby groups consecutive equal items: for each run it gives the item and an iterator over the run.
The run is an iterator, not a list: count it with sum(1 for _ in run) or len(list(run)).
For decode, character * length repeats a character, and ''.join joins the pieces.

wordings.title: Sort by several fields
wordings.statement:
Write `sort_records(records, keys)`. `records` is a list of dicts, and `keys` a list of
field names. Return a new list of the records sorted by the first key, records equal in
it by the second, and so on. A name that starts with `-` sorts its field in descending
order. Records equal in every key keep their order. `records` itself doesn't change.

A field has values of one type in all records, numbers or strings.
constraints: Field names don't start with -, and every record has every field in keys

problems.reference_solution:
from operator import itemgetter


def sort_records(records, keys):
    """Return records sorted by keys in order; a key starting with - sorts descending."""
    result = list(records)
    # Sorting is stable, so sorting by the last key first leaves the first key in charge.
    for key in reversed(keys):
        descending = key.startswith('-')
        result.sort(key=itemgetter(key[1:] if descending else key), reverse=descending)
    return result
problems.tests:
import random

from solution import *

PEOPLE = [
    {'name': 'b', 'age': 30, 'city': 'Rome'},
    {'name': 'a', 'age': 30, 'city': 'Oslo'},
    {'name': 'c', 'age': 25, 'city': 'Rome'},
    {'name': 'd', 'age': 25, 'city': 'Oslo'},
]


def _names(records):
    return [record['name'] for record in records]


def test_example_1():
    """Age descending, then name ascending."""
    records = [{'name': 'b', 'age': 30}, {'name': 'a', 'age': 30}, {'name': 'c', 'age': 25}]
    assert sort_records(records, ['-age', 'name']) == [
        {'name': 'a', 'age': 30},
        {'name': 'b', 'age': 30},
        {'name': 'c', 'age': 25},
    ]


def test_descending_strings():
    """A string field in descending order."""
    assert _names(sort_records(PEOPLE, ['-city', 'age'])) == ['c', 'b', 'd', 'a']


def test_stable():
    """Records equal in every key keep their order."""
    assert _names(sort_records(PEOPLE, ['age'])) == ['c', 'd', 'b', 'a']
    assert _names(sort_records(PEOPLE, ['-age'])) == ['b', 'a', 'c', 'd']


def test_no_keys():
    """No keys: the same order, in a new list."""
    result = sort_records(PEOPLE, [])
    assert result == PEOPLE and result is not PEOPLE


def test_input_unchanged():
    """The given list keeps its order."""
    records = list(PEOPLE)
    sort_records(records, ['name'])
    assert records == PEOPLE


def test_random():
    """Random records, compared pair by pair."""
    rng = random.Random(6)
    records = [
        {'id': i, 'team': rng.choice('xyz'), 'score': rng.randint(0, 5), 'tag': rng.choice(['p', 'q'])}
        for i in range(20000)
    ]
    result = sort_records(records, ['team', '-score', '-tag'])
    assert sorted(r['id'] for r in result) == list(range(20000))
    for a, b in zip(result, result[1:]):
        key_a = (a['team'], -a['score'], a['tag'] == 'p')
        key_b = (b['team'], -b['score'], b['tag'] == 'p')
        assert key_a < key_b or (key_a == key_b and a['id'] < b['id'])
hints: Negating a value sorts numbers in reverse, but not strings. sort and sorted take reverse=True instead.
Python's sort is stable, and stays stable with reverse=True. Sorting by the last key first, then the one before it, and so on, gives the order of all keys.
operator.itemgetter('age') is a key function that reads record['age']. functools.cmp_to_key is another way: one comparison function over all keys.
problems.summary: Multi-key sorts with itemgetter and stable sorting

wordings.text: Which operations take O(1) time on a `collections.deque` `d` of n items?

questions.explanation:
A deque adds and removes at both ends in O(1). Reading an item by index is O(1) near the
ends but O(n) in the middle. A list is the other way round: O(1) indexing, but O(n)
insert(0, x) and pop(0).
questions.summary: Which deque operations are constant time

wordings.text:
What does this print?

```python
from collections import defaultdict

counts = defaultdict(int)
if counts['x'] == 0:
    pass
print(len(counts), 'y' in counts)
```

questions.explanation:
Reading a missing key of a defaultdict creates it with the default, so counts['x']
adds x with 0. The in test doesn't create keys. Use counts.get('x', 0) to read without
adding.
questions.summary: Reading a missing key adds it to a defaultdict

wordings.text: After `h = [5, 1, 4, 2, 3]` and `heapq.heapify(h)`, what is guaranteed?
options: `h[0]` is 1, and the rest is in heap order, not necessarily sorted

questions.explanation:
heapq keeps a min-heap in a list: each item is at most its children, at 2i + 1 and
2i + 2. Only h[0] is fixed, as the smallest; the rest can be in several orders. For a
max-heap, push negated values.
questions.summary: What heapify guarantees

wordings.text:
What happens here?

```python
import heapq

h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (1, {'job': 'a'}))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, {'job': 'b'}))
```
options: TypeError: the priorities are equal, so the dicts are compared
The second push replaces the first
Both are pushed, ordered by the time they arrived
Both are pushed, ordered by job name

questions.explanation:
Tuples compare item by item. With equal priorities, the next items, two dicts, are
compared, and dicts don't support <. Put a counter between them, (priority, count,
item), so ties never reach the item and come out in arrival order.
questions.summary: Equal priorities in a heap compare the next item

wordings.text: For `a = [1, 2, 2, 3]`, what are `bisect_left(a, 2)` and `bisect_right(a, 2)`?

questions.explanation:
bisect_left returns the first index where 2 could be inserted keeping the order, before
the existing 2s; bisect_right the last, after them. Their difference, 2, is how many 2s
there are.
questions.summary: bisect_left and bisect_right around equal values

wordings.text: What does `bisect.insort(a, x)` cost on a sorted list of n items?
options: O(log n) comparisons, but O(n) time in all, since later items shift
O(n log n), since it sorts the list again

questions.explanation:
insort finds the position by binary search, then inserts there, which moves every later
item one place. The shift is a fast memory move, so insort works well for moderate
sizes, but it is still linear.
questions.summary: The cost of insort

wordings.text: What is `[key for key, _ in itertools.groupby('aabaa')]`?

questions.explanation:
groupby groups consecutive equal items, so the two runs of a stay apart. To group all
equal items, sort them first.
questions.summary: groupby groups only consecutive items

wordings.text: How many tuples do `itertools.combinations(range(5), 2)` and `itertools.permutations(range(5), 2)` give?

questions.explanation:
combinations ignores order: 5 choose 2 is 10. permutations counts each order: 5 × 4 is
20. 25 is product(range(5), repeat=2), which also pairs an item with itself.
questions.summary: Counting combinations and permutations

wordings.text: What is `functools.reduce(lambda acc, digit: acc * 10 + digit, [1, 2, 3])`?

questions.explanation:
reduce starts with the first item as acc and folds in the rest: 1 * 10 + 2 is 12, and
12 * 10 + 3 is 123. With an empty list and no initial value, reduce raises TypeError.
questions.summary: Folding a list with reduce and a lambda

options: TypeError: a list can't be hashed, and the cache keys on the arguments
It returns 3, and later calls with a changed list return the old result

questions.explanation:
lru_cache stores results in a dict keyed by the arguments, so they must be hashable.
Pass a tuple instead. Caching on a mutable argument would be unsafe anyway: the list
could change after its result was stored.
questions.summary: lru_cache needs hashable arguments

wordings.text: What do `re.match(r'\d+', 'ab12')` and `re.search(r'\d+', 'ab12')` give?

questions.explanation:
re.match only matches at the start of the string, which is a letter here. re.search
looks for the first match anywhere. re.fullmatch needs the whole string to match.
questions.summary: re.match anchors at the start, re.search does not

wordings.text: What is `re.findall(r'<.+>', '<a><b>')`?

questions.explanation:
.+ is greedy: it takes as much as it can and gives back only what the closing > needs,
so the match runs to the last >. The lazy .+? stops at the first >, giving ['<a>',
'<b>'].
questions.summary: Greedy and lazy quantifiers

wordings.text: What is `json.dumps({1: (2, 3), 'ok': None})`?

questions.explanation:
JSON object keys are strings, so 1 becomes "1"; tuples become arrays, and None becomes
null. json.loads won't give back the same dict: the key stays "1" and the tuple is a
list.
questions.summary: How Python values map to JSON

wordings.text: Why read CSV with the `csv` module instead of `line.split(',')`?
options: A quoted field can contain commas
A quoted field can contain line breaks

questions.explanation:
CSV quotes fields that contain commas, quotes or line breaks, and doubles quotes inside
them; split knows none of this. csv.reader still returns every field as a string, and
'a,,b'.split(',') keeps the empty field.
questions.summary: What the csv module handles that split does not

wordings.text: `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is False. Why, and what is the usual fix?
options: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so the sum is slightly off; compare with `math.isclose`
Python rounds floats to 15 digits when adding; compare with `round`
`==` compares identity for floats; compare with `is`
The sum is a Decimal; convert it with `float`

questions.explanation:
Floats are binary fractions, and 0.1 can't be written exactly in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2
is 0.30000000000000004. math.isclose allows a small relative difference. For exact
decimal money, use decimal.Decimal.
questions.summary: Comparing floats with math.isclose

wordings.text: Which call gives 3 different items of the list `cards`, picked at random?

questions.explanation:
sample picks without replacement. choices picks with replacement, so items can repeat.
shuffle reorders the list in place and returns None, and choice returns one item.
random.seed(n) makes the picks repeatable.
questions.summary: Picking without replacement with random.sample

wordings.text:
What happens here?

```python
from datetime import datetime, timezone

aware = datetime(2024, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
naive = datetime(2024, 1, 1)
aware - naive
```
options: TypeError: naive and aware datetimes can't be subtracted
It gives the local time zone's offset

questions.explanation:
A naive datetime has no time zone, so Python can't tell which moment it is and refuses
to mix it with an aware one; comparing them for order raises too. Keep times aware,
usually in UTC, and convert for display.
questions.summary: Naive and aware datetimes don't mix

wordings.text: For `d = timedelta(hours=25)`, what are `d.days` and `d.seconds`?

questions.explanation:
A timedelta is stored as days, seconds below a day and microseconds. 25 hours is 1 day
and 3,600 seconds. d.seconds is not the total: d.total_seconds() gives 90000.0.
questions.summary: timedelta keeps days and seconds apart

wordings.text: Which of these make a new list with the same items as the list `a`?

questions.explanation:
Slicing, list() and copy.copy all make a shallow copy: a new list holding the same item
objects. b = a makes no list at all; it gives the same list a second name.
questions.summary: Ways to make a shallow copy

wordings.text:
What does this print?

```python
import copy

inner = [1]
pair = [inner, inner]
clone = copy.deepcopy(pair)
clone[0].append(2)
print(clone[1], inner)
```

questions.explanation:
deepcopy remembers what it has already copied, so an object shared inside the original
is copied once and shared in the copy too: clone[0] and clone[1] are one new list. The
original inner list is untouched.
questions.summary: deepcopy keeps shared objects shared

wordings.text: For `class Color(Enum): RED = 1`, which of these are True?

questions.summary: Looking up enum members by value and name

wordings.text:
What does this print?

```python
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    ACTIVE = 1
    RUNNING = 1
    DONE = 2

print(len(Status), Status.RUNNING)
```

questions.explanation:
A second name with the same value becomes an alias of the first member, not a member of
its own: iteration and len skip it, and it refers to ACTIVE. The @unique decorator turns
aliases into a ValueError.
questions.summary: Repeated values make enum aliases

wordings.text: For `p = Path('/data/logs/app.tar.gz')`, what are `p.name`, `p.suffix` and `p.stem`?

questions.explanation:
name is the last part of the path. suffix is only the last extension, and stem is the
name without it. p.suffixes gives ['.tar', '.gz'], and p.parent is /data/logs.
questions.summary: Parts of a path in pathlib

wordings.text:
What does this print?

```python
import io

buffer = io.StringIO()
buffer.write('hello')
print(repr(buffer.read()), repr(buffer.getvalue()))
```

questions.explanation:
A StringIO works like an open file with one position: after writing, the position is at
the end, so read() returns nothing. buffer.seek(0) moves back to the start. getvalue()
returns the whole contents wherever the position is.
questions.summary: Reading a StringIO after writing to it
